pass_a_gloss: And still a human being also loves living, having taken a persuasion about the being of a reasoning soul as having something kindred to God. For both are mind-like and unseen and, as the prevailing reasoning shows, without body. And why did the one equipping us make in us a yearning for the reverence toward him and the communion, which even in the ones who have slipped keeps certain footprints of the divine wish, if the thing by nature yearned for were not possible and reachable for the reasoning ones to seize? And plain it is that, just as each limb of ours is grown toward something to keep an at-homeness, the eyes toward the visible things and ears toward the hearable things, so mind toward the thought-objects and the God beyond the thought-objects. Why then do we delay and doubt, having laid aside the obstructing perishable body, making heavy a soul, weighing down a mind of many cares, an earthy tent, to be loosed from the bonds and to unmoor from the waves with flesh and blood? So that together with Christ Jesus we may rest the rest proper to the blessedness, gazing on the same, whole through wholes, ensouled Word, and being nourished from him and seizing the most many-coloured wisdom in him and being moulded by the self-truth, and in the true and unceasing light of the knowing being shone down upon as to the mind, toward the beholding of the things born to be beheld through that light, by eyes being lit by the commandment of the Lord.
pass_b_english: Further, a man also loves life once he has been convinced about the essence of the rational soul, that it has something akin to God. For both are intellectual and invisible, and, as the prevailing argument shows, incorporeal. And why did he who fashioned us plant in us a longing for godliness towards him and for fellowship with him, a longing that keeps some traces of the divine will even in those who have gone astray, if it were not possible and within reach for rational beings to lay hold of what they naturally long for? It is clear that, just as each of our members is made by nature to keep a certain affinity with something, the eyes with what is seen and the ears with what is heard, so the mind is made for what is intelligible and for the God who is beyond the intelligible.

Why then do we shrink and hesitate to put off the “corruptible body” that hinders us, that “weighs down the soul”, the “earthly tent” that burdens “the anxious mind” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15), to be set free from our bonds and to depart from the waves that go with flesh and blood? We would do it so that with Christ Jesus we may rest the rest that belongs to blessedness: contemplating the Word, the same, whole and alive throughout; being fed by him; grasping the richly varied wisdom in him; being stamped by Truth itself; and having our minds lit by the true and unfailing light of knowledge, so as to behold the things that by nature are seen through that light, with eyes enlightened by the Lord's commandment (Psalm 19:8).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 47); the old English was a digest: the published English for this chapter was the house on the rock and 1 Corinthians 9:26-27 (ch. 48), with nothing from ch. 47's argument on the soul's kinship with God.
'εἷς ἐχούσης' read as 'ὡς ἐχούσης'; '6 κατασκευάζων' as 'ὁ κατασκευάζων'; 'σῴξ δεεν' as 'σῴζειν'; 'ἕνα σὺν Χριστῷ' as 'ἵνα σὺν Χριστῷ'; 'di’ ὅλων' as 'δι᾽ ὅλων'; 'φοτιζομένων' as 'φωτιζομένων'.
The purpose clause is kept as purpose ('so that ... we may rest'), opened with 'We would do it' because the question before it is a separate English sentence; the participles stay as participles.
